stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Slide $Z$ (protons) and $N$ (neutrons) to build a nucleus. Watch the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve ($E_\ell / A$) and the two force bars: the short-range strong attraction and the long-range Coulomb repulsion. Advance after visiting $6$ different elements.
stages.concept: Every nucleus is held together by the short-range strong nuclear force acting between neighbouring nucleons. It is opposed by Coulomb repulsion between protons, which grows with $Z^2$. The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve $E_\ell / A$ measures how tightly each nucleon is bound; its peak near $A \approx 56$ (iron) marks the most stable region.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Build each named target nucleus by setting $Z$ and $N$. Compare where each target sits on the $E_\ell / A$ curve and how the two force bars balance.
stages.concept: Light nuclei sit on the rising side of the curve — fusing them releases energy. Heavy nuclei sit on the falling side — splitting them (fission) releases energy. Iron sits at the peak: it is the endpoint of both processes.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Force bars and curve marker are hidden. Given $Z$ and $N$, decide where the nucleus sits on the $E_\ell / A$ curve: rising side, peak, or falling side. You must answer all correctly in one pass — a wrong answer restarts the deck.
stages.concept: Rule of thumb: $A < 20$ is on the rising side (fusion territory); $A \approx 50$–$70$ is at the peak (iron / nickel); $A > 100$ is on the falling side (fission territory). Compute $A = Z + N$, then place it on the curve.

labels.where_on_curve: where does this nucleus sit on the E_l / A curve?
labels.peek_tip: Compute A = Z + N. Rule of thumb: A below 20 = rising side (fusion); A between 50 and 70 = peak (iron/nickel); A above 100 = falling side (fission). Do not look at the curve — reason from A alone.
labels.tip1: slide Z and N — visit light, medium, and heavy elements
labels.tip2: match each target; compare where it sits on the curve
labels.tip3: compute A = Z + N, then place it on the curve

1.1: Try light nuclei first: hydrogen (Z=1), helium (Z=2), carbon (Z=6), oxygen (Z=8).
1.2: Then medium nuclei: iron (Z=26), nickel (Z=28). Notice the E_l/A curve peaks there.
1.3: Finally heavy nuclei: lead (Z=82), uranium (Z=92). The curve comes back down — heavy nuclei are less tightly bound per nucleon.

2.1: For Helium-4 set Z=2 and N=2. It sits low on the rising side of the curve — light nuclei are less bound per nucleon.
2.2: For Iron-56 set Z=26 and N=30. This is the peak: the most tightly bound nucleon on average.
2.3: For Uranium-235 set Z=92 and N=143. Watch the Coulomb bar grow — heavy nuclei are less bound because proton repulsion catches up.

3.1: Only A matters for this classification. Compute A = Z + N first.
3.2: A below 20 → rising side (fusion territory). A above 100 → falling side (fission territory).
3.3: The peak is narrow: only nuclei near A = 50 to 70 count as 'peak'. Everything else is either rising or falling.
